extracted.intended_audience: patent analysts, USPTO staff, researchers and policymakers conducting patent landscaping and patent-data diffusion studies
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and analyze the volume, component technologies, and diffusion of AI-related inventions using U.S. patent data and a machine-learning classification approach, with manual validation and benchmarking against query-based methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge processing (AI component)
rubrics_metrics.description: The field of knowledge processing involves representing and deriving facts about the world and using this information in automated systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: U.S. Patent No. 7,685,082 (Intuit) describes an algorithm using a pre-defined "knowledge base" to detect accounting errors (real-time error detection for online income tax preparation). A patent document may contain knowledge processing alongside other AI components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech (AI component)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech recognition techniques to understand a sequence of words given an acoustic signal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: U.S. Patent No. 10,043,516 (Apple) describes an "Intelligent automated assistant" like Siri/Alexa/Cortana. Patents classified in speech can be used as exemplars for speech-recognition functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI hardware (AI component)
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical computer components designed to meet computing power requirements of AI through increased processing efficiency and/or speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: U.S. Patent No. 8,892,487 (IBM) describes hardware mimicking synapses. AI-hardware patents often correlate with increases in compute-intensive AI applications like vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary computation (AI component)
rubrics_metrics.description: Computational routines using aspects of nature and evolution (e.g., genetic algorithms) to evaluate competing models and select high-performance models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: U.S. Patent No. 7,657,494 (Chevron) uses genetically inspired mutation of models to predict petroleum reserves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural language processing (AI component)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods for understanding and using data encoded in written language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: U.S. Patent No. 8,930,178 (Cincinnati Children's Hospital) builds ontologies from text for healthcare administrative tasks like billing-code assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine learning (AI component)
rubrics_metrics.description: Models that learn from data to perform tasks such as classification, prediction, or optimization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: U.S. Patent No. 9,390,378 (Wal‑Mart) develops algorithms to optimize e-commerce by classifying product descriptions and resolving ambiguity via crowdsourcing. Machine-learning patents often co-occur with planning/control or knowledge processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vision (AI component)
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer vision methods for extracting and understanding information from images and videos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: U.S. Patent No. 10,055,843 (Mayo Foundation / ASU) automates detection of abnormalities in colonoscopy images. Vision patents have shown marked growth since 2012 and are associated with increased AI hardware patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning and control (AI component)
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes to identify, create, and execute activities to achieve specified goals (control systems, workflow management, expert systems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: U.S. Patent No. 10,031,490 (Fisher‑Rosemount) detects abnormal conditions and uses an expert system to identify and address problems; planning/control and knowledge processing diffuse fastest across technology subclasses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow multiple component classifications per patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A single patent document may contain multiple AI component technologies and thus be classified into more than one component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use per-component classifiers and also consolidate to an "any AI" indicator that flags a patent if it belongs to at least one component technology (e.g., a patent could be both machine learning and AI hardware).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-learning classification approach for patent landscaping
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat patent landscaping as a binary classification problem and create separate classifiers for each of the eight AI components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: (1) generate seed and anti-seed sets, (2) train neural-network classifiers using patent text and citations, (3) apply classifiers to patent universe to predict component membership, (4) consolidate component predictions to create 'any AI' indicator. The USPTO used optimal neural-network models as in Abood and Feltenberger (2018).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seed set construction (training positives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a seed set representing documents that comprise the technology using narrow search queries (keywords/classifications) to ensure relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seed sets should be narrowly defined so results are relevant even if too small for a full landscape; seed set quality was validated (92% of seed documents contained at least one AI component in USPTO work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-seed set construction (training negatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create an anti-seed set representing documents unrelated to the technology, typically via an 'expansion' procedure and random sampling from unrelated documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality anti-seed generation is critical to train classifiers; USPTO achieved ~93% of anti-seed documents containing no AI component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training data fields for classifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use patent abstract and claims text plus forward and backward patent citations as input features for machine-learning classifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include non-patent references in model inputs (USPTO approach excluded non-patent references). This choice shapes classifier performance and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual validation protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Validate machine predictions with manual review: draw a random sample, have experienced examiners label documents, and use adjudication for disagreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO: random sample of 800 documents; each document reviewed by exactly two examiners; a third examiner adjudicated disagreements; examiners were provided training materials defining each AI component and examples; resulting manual labels form a gold standard for model evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics and definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use precision, recall, F1 score, and accuracy to benchmark classifier performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precision = % of predicted-AI documents that are actually AI; Recall = % of actual AI documents predicted as AI; F1 = harmonic mean of precision and recall (balances the tradeoff); Accuracy = % of all correct predictions. Note the tradeoff—higher recall can reduce precision and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmarking and comparison best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing models/landscapes, exclude seed and anti-seed documents from evaluation to avoid optimistic bias and compare against alternative approaches and baselines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO compared its model against recreated Cockburn (2019), WIPO (2019), manual scoring, and a naive all-not-AI baseline; the report stresses that query-based approaches can have low recall and that naive classifiers can show misleading accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of PatentsView for disambiguation and linking
rubrics_metrics.description: Link granted patents to PatentsView identifiers to obtain unique inventor, owner-at-grant, and location IDs for diffusion analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PatentsView provides unique IDs to avoid miscounting due to name variation (e.g., 'International Business Machines' vs 'IBM'). The USPTO analysis relied on PatentsView for inventor-patentee and owner-at-grant identifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diffusion metrics for AI across technologies, inventors, owners, and geography
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure AI diffusion using multiple complementary metrics: annual volume and share of public AI patent applications; percentage of technology subclasses containing AI (e.g., share of subclasses with ≥2 AI patents); annual percentage of inventor-patentees and owners-at-grant with at least one AI patent; geographic concentration maps and county-level counts; top AI patent owners and concentration shares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret diffusion broadly (across technology subclasses, inventors, organizations, geography). Example: report tracks growth in AI patent applications (2002–2018), spread from ~9% to ~16% share of applications, and diffusion across subclasses from ~9% in 1976 to >42% in 2018. Use thresholds (e.g., ≥2 granted AI patents in a subclass) for inclusion when mapping diffusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of time index and public vs granted documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Define time-series year carefully: use earliest U.S. publication year (either first pre-grant publication or granted patent publication) for public-application time series; grant year may be used for other analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of policy-induced discontinuities (e.g., American Inventors Protection Act implementation around 1999 increased pre-grant publications and the volume of publicly available patent applications). Adjust interpretation accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-scope and owner-at-grant focus (limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing patent owners, focus on owners listed at grant (owners-at-grant) and note limitations from post-grant transfers and missing comprehensive post-grant assignment data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners-at-grant may include inventors who did not assign rights; the dataset excludes later transfers, so diffusion across organizations post-grant is not captured. Reporters should state these limitations explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation guidance about component diffusion clusters
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize clusters of AI components that diffuse at different rates (e.g., knowledge processing and planning/control diffuse fastest; vision, machine learning, and AI hardware diffuse more slowly but increasing; evolutionary computation, speech, NLP diffuse slowest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these cluster observations as hypotheses about technological interdependence; caution that more research is needed to understand causal drivers of differing diffusion rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of query-based vs machine-learning approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional query-based landscaping (keywords, limited classes) can be overly narrow and miss many AI-relevant patents, reducing recall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO found Cockburn et al. (2019) and recreated WIPO (2019) had low recall compared to their ML approach. Use ML methods to flexibly learn from document text to improve recall, with manual validation to assess precision.
